findings.claim: The model answer defines Garrafeira as three to six years in wood, then at least eight years in glass demijohns, and says Niepoort is effectively the only producer.
findings.finalFix: Garrafeira is a rare and legally distinct single-vintage category. Under the IVDP rules of 2022 it spends four to eight years in wood, then further ageing in glass (in practice large demijohns, the bonbonnes), with a 15-year minimum set by the IVDP, so it cannot reach the market until at least 15 years after the harvest; the label shows both the harvest year and the year of final bottling. The glass halts oxidative development and gives a nutty, delicate, almost Colheita-like wine with a fine soft deposit. Niepoort kept the category alive and pressed for the 2022 definition; Niepoort and Quevedo are the houses making it today.

findings.claim: The explanation says Garrafeira is 'the only Port style deliberately matured in a vessel that admits no oxygen'.
findings.finalFix: Both exist to test whether you have read the IVDP's category list rather than a shipper's marketing. Garrafeira is also conceptually interesting: it is the only Port style that follows years of oxidative ageing in wood with a long reductive rest in large glass demijohns before bottling, which is why it tastes unlike any cask-aged tawny of comparable age.
